name: biosig
desc: Tools for biomedical signal processing and data conversion
why: Biomedical signal conversion tools for EEG and ECG formats; real science, but the niche is narrow and the tools are file converters.

brief.what_it_is: BioSig is an open source software library for biomedical signal processing, covering biosignals such as EEG, ECoG, ECG, EOG, EMG and respiration. The homepage describes it as several parts: a toolbox for Octave and Matlab with data import/export filters, feature extraction, classification and a viewing and scoring tool; a C/C++ library with reading and writing routines for many biosignal data formats; rtsBCI, a real-time BCI system in Matlab and Simulink; and BioProFeed and BCIx, which the homepage lists without description. The executables you scouted (bin2rec, biosig2gdf, save2gdf, save2scp and others) are not named on the pages I read, so I could not confirm their individual functions. The data-conversion angle is real, but the homepage presents BioSig as a much broader signal-processing toolkit.
brief.why_it_exists: The aim of the BioSig project is to foster research in biomedical signal processing by providing open source software tools for many different applications. The homepage says the field needs solutions for data acquisition, artifact processing, quality control, feature extraction, classification, modeling and visualization, and that BioSig tries to cover them.

brief.standout: BioSig covers many biosignal formats through one library and is free under GPL, with bindings across Octave, Matlab, C/C++, Python, Java, R and Mathematica. Its file-format converters are part of a much wider research toolkit that also includes a real-time BCI system and a viewer.

entry.title: BioSig
entry.tldr: An open source library and set of converters for EEG, ECG and other biosignal file formats, built so researchers can read and write each other's recordings.
entry.deeper_look:
BioSig is a research toolkit for biomedical signals: EEG, ECoG, ECG, EOG, EMG, respiration and similar recordings. The core is a C/C++ library that reads and writes many biosignal data formats. Around it sit bindings and tools for Octave, Matlab, Python, Java, R and Mathematica, plus a real-time brain-computer interface system called rtsBCI and a viewer and scoring tool.

The Homebrew formula installs the library and a handful of command-line programs with names like `biosig2gdf`, `save2gdf`, `save2scp`, `save2aecg` and `heka2itx`. The names suggest format converters, for example to GDF, SCP-ECG and aECG. The brief did not confirm what each one does, so check their `--help` output before relying on a guess.

The project's stated aim is "to foster research in biomedical signal processing by providing open source software tools for many different applications." Labs record in different vendors' formats, and data acquisition, artifact processing, quality control, feature extraction, classification and visualization all depend on being able to open the file first. A shared reader library removes that obstacle.

The door here is the signal-processing field itself. Once a recording opens, you can see how brain and heart signals are stored, annotated and passed between tools. That is a long way into a field, and the converters are only the first step.
entry.install:
brew install biosig
# The Python package needs libbiosig installed first: pip install biosig
# Viewer via the project's tap: brew install schloegl/biosig/sigviewer

Prints usage for the GDF saving tool, so you can see which input formats and options it accepts.
Installs SigViewer, a viewer for biosignal recordings with GDF event file import and export.

entry.whats_unique: One GPL library reads many biosignal file formats, with bindings across Octave, Matlab, Python, Java, R and Mathematica. It also sits beside a real-time brain-computer interface system and a viewer.
entry.caveats: You need your own recordings to do anything interesting, and the brief did not show usage text for the executables. Some components, such as the Octave and Matlab packages, are older than the core library.
